```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

An effect plot isolates one contribution to a model. It helps explain how the
model works, but it need not show the expected response. This distinction
matters especially with interactions, random effects and nonlinear links. We
use the plant experiment from [Smooth trends and repeated measurements with
glmmTMB](glmmTMB-support.html) to explore flexible individual curves, then daily
air quality measurements to read interaction surfaces.

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library("mgcv")
library("gratia")
library("ggplot2")
```

## Do plants need different curve shapes?

The carbon dioxide experiment has seven measurements on each of twelve plants,
with three plants in each origin-treatment combination. Positive uptake and
increasing residual spread motivate a Gamma model with a log link. A shared
smooth captures saturation with increasing concentration. We now allow
plant-specific *smooth* deviations, rather than the straight-line deviations
used in the glmmTMB article.

```{r plant-flexible-fit}
plant <- as.data.frame(CO2)
plant$Plant <- factor(plant$Plant, ordered = FALSE)
plant$log_conc <- log(plant$conc) - mean(log(plant$conc))
plant_gam <- gam(
  uptake ~ Type * Treatment + s(log_conc, k = 5) +
    t2(log_conc, Plant, bs = c("cr", "re"), k = c(4, 12), full = TRUE),
  data = plant, family = Gamma(link = "log"), method = "REML")
overview(plant_gam)
```

The tensor product combines a cubic regression spline over concentration with
a random-effect basis over plants. It penalises plant-specific departures and
shares information across plants. `full = TRUE` keeps separate penalties for
the parts of this tensor construction. With only seven observations per plant,
the small concentration basis is deliberate. Each plant's concentration
contribution is the sum of the common curve and its smooth deviation. The
intercept, origin and treatment terms supply the remaining contributions
to its fitted log uptake.

```{r plant-tensor-curves}
smooths(plant_gam)
draw(plant_gam, select = "t2(log_conc,Plant)",
  re_levels = list(Plant = c("Qn1", "Qn2", "Qn3")),
  xlab = "Centred log concentration", ylab = "Plant contribution to log uptake") &
  theme(legend.position = "right") & labs(colour = "Plant")
```

The numeric covariate is always the horizontal axis even if the factor was
specified first in the tensor formula. `re_levels` chooses plants by name;
it does not refit the model or remove their contributions from predictions.
The fitted factor ordering is retained. Selecting plants of one treatment
makes the variation among biological replicates visible. Treatment comparisons
require the origin and treatment terms as well as these plant deviations.

```{r plant-full-curves}
plant$mean_uptake <- fitted(plant_gam)
ggplot(plant, aes(conc, uptake, group = Plant, colour = Treatment)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(aes(y = mean_uptake)) +
  facet_wrap(~ Type) +
  labs(x = "Carbon dioxide concentration (mL/L)",
    y = expression(CO[2] ~ uptake ~ (mu * mol ~ m^{-2} ~ s^{-1})))
```

The model explains rapid increases and subsequent flattening in these observed
plants. This is conditional on their fitted deviations, rather than a forecast
for a new plant. The smooth deviations allow each plant's curve to bend,
whereas straight random slopes only change its tilt. For treatment comparisons,
each plant supplies one independent curve: three replicates per origin and
treatment combination.

```{r plant-variance-components}
variance_comp(plant_gam)
```

These are variance components in the random-effect representation of the
penalised splines. Different tensor components can have different estimated
variances, so one variance alone does not describe all plant-curve variation.
The spline rows are not observation variances; the `scale` row estimates Gamma
dispersion, which multiplies the squared mean to give response variance.
Fits selected by GCV may lack
confidence intervals; the estimates remain available. A model with no
extractable variance components returns an empty table.

Tensor plots follow the same principle in higher dimensions. Two continuous
covariates make a surface; additional numerical dimensions become conditioning
slices and factor dimensions become facets. `n_2d` controls each surface axis,
while `n_3d` and `n_4d` limit conditioning dimensions. The latter also limit
factor levels to the first levels in fitted order. Use named `re_levels` or
explicit evaluation `data` to choose meaningful groups. With two factor
margins, the display is categorical estimates and intervals, faceted by the
second factor; there is no numeric axis to interpolate between categories.
These rules apply to `te()`, `ti()` and `t2()` random-effect tensor terms.

## Is the temperature association different on calm and windy days?

The `airquality` data contain daily New York measurements from May to September
1973. Ozone is in parts per billion, temperature in degrees Fahrenheit, wind
speed in miles per hour, and solar radiation in Langleys; see
`?datasets::airquality` for the sources. We retain complete cases, so our
analysis uses the days with all needed measurements.

The question is whether ozone's association with temperature depends on wind,
and whether that relationship is stable across summer months. We model log
ozone with a Gaussian distribution, allow a smooth association with solar
radiation, and use a temperature-by-wind-by-month interaction.

```{r ozone-fit}
ozone <- na.omit(airquality[c("Ozone", "Solar.R", "Wind", "Temp", "Month")])
ozone$month <- factor(ozone$Month, labels = month.abb[5:9])
ozone_gam <- gam(log(Ozone) ~ s(Solar.R, k = 6) + Temp * Wind * month,
  data = ozone, method = "REML")
table(ozone$month)
overview(ozone_gam)
```

A three-way interaction gives each month its own temperature-by-wind surface.
That flexibility makes the model useful for exploring stability, but estimates
in sparsely sampled parts of a month's weather range may be imprecise. Inspect
the distribution of observations before interpreting a surface:

```{r ozone-support}
ggplot(ozone, aes(Temp, Wind, colour = Ozone)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ month) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (degrees F)", y = "Wind speed (mph)",
    colour = "Ozone (ppb)")
```

## Start with the interaction, then reconstruct the model

```{r ozone-numeric-interaction}
parametric_terms(ozone_gam)
weather_effect <- parametric_effects(ozone_gam, terms = "Temp:Wind", n_2d = 30)
draw(weather_effect, surface = "tile") &
  labs(x = "Temperature (degrees F)", y = "Wind speed (mph)")
```

This surface shows the coefficient-weighted temperature-by-wind contribution
for the reference month, May. Its colours are partial contributions to **log**
ozone. They exclude the intercept, the temperature and wind main effects, the
solar smooth, and other interaction terms. The diverging palette centres at
zero, making the contribution's sign visible. To interpret the complete
temperature association, combine this interaction with the main temperature
effect and the monthly adjustments below.

`surface = "tile"` uses vector rectangles, which can be useful in a vector
figure. The default `"raster"` keeps large plots compact. `n_2d = 30` evaluates
30 points along each surface axis, rather than borrowing the 100-point curve
resolution. Increase `n_2d` when you need a finer display of the same fitted
surface.

```{r ozone-month-interactions, fig.height = 7}
draw(parametric_effects(ozone_gam, terms = "Temp:Wind:month", n_2d = 25),
  surface = "tile") &
  labs(x = "Temperature (degrees F)", y = "Wind speed (mph)")
```

The additional monthly contributions appear in conditioning facets. Under
treatment contrast coding the reference month's contribution is zero. The
other panels are adjustments to the May interaction, not complete monthly
surfaces. Fill limits are shared across facets and centred at zero. If a
surface varies mainly because of poor covariate support, masking helps avoid
giving extrapolation the same visual prominence as interpolation: `dist`
uses distance after scaling the displayed axes into the unit square. Support
is pooled across months, so a location left visible may still lie outside an
individual month's observed weather conditions. Use the monthly observation
plot above to decide which parts of each surface have local data support.

Numeric-by-factor interactions are grouped curves rather than surfaces:

```{r ozone-numeric-factor}
draw(parametric_effects(ozone_gam, terms = "Temp:month")) &
  labs(x = "Temperature (degrees F)", y = "Additional contribution to log ozone")
```

These slopes must be combined with the reference temperature slope and the
wind interactions to describe the model's temperature association. The
[conditional comparisons article](prediction-comparisons.html) shows how to
compare complete fitted values without isolating contrast-coded terms.

For a direct view of the complete model, predict at observed weather conditions:

```{r ozone-full-predictions}
ozone$fitted_log <- fitted(ozone_gam)
ggplot(ozone, aes(log(Ozone), fitted_log, colour = month)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Observed log ozone", y = "Fitted log ozone", colour = "Month")
```

The fitted values concern mean **log** ozone. Exponentiating them gives the
conditional median under the lognormal assumption, not the arithmetic mean
ozone concentration. The observed-versus-fitted plot shows how the combined
terms reproduce log ozone on the sampled days. Because these are daily
measurements, also check residuals in time order: remaining serial dependence
would affect uncertainty in the monthly comparisons.

## Choose a display without changing its statistical meaning

The optional ggcube package can show the same numerical surface in three
dimensions:

```{r ozone-3d}
if (requireNamespace("ggcube", quietly = TRUE)) {
  draw(weather_effect, surface = "3d",
    surface_3d = list(yaw = 35, persp = FALSE)) &
    labs(x = "Temperature (degrees F)", y = "Wind speed (mph)")
}
```

Height and fill both represent the same partial contribution. A three-dimensional
view can emphasise its shape, while a flat surface is often easier to compare
across months. View settings change the rendering, not estimates or uncertainty.
Curves, factor estimates and spherical maps retain their usual displays. The
conditional chunk runs only when ggcube is installed; the flat plots contain
the complete analysis.

Parametric effect coordinates now use the model's covariate scale by default.
For example, a term involving `log(x)` uses `log(x)` on the horizontal axis.
`back_transform = TRUE` displays original covariate coordinates without
changing effect values or intervals. With saved smooth estimates, prepare
them using `smooth_estimates(model, back_transform = TRUE)` before asking
`draw()` to use that scale. See [Transformed covariates](transformed-covariates.html)
for worked examples, including functions without analytic inverses.

Effect intervals include uncertainty in their model intercept by default,
including its covariance with a parametric term. Setting
`overall_uncertainty = FALSE` changes that uncertainty calculation without
adding or subtracting the intercept from the displayed partial contribution.
For contrasts between complete model predictions, use a method that includes
all relevant terms and their covariance rather than subtracting interval
endpoints from these plots.
